1956009086723518773 [2025-08-14] @TylerAlterman 💜 1052 🔁 98
I always wondered how my NYC community would perform in an emergency situation. We got a test of that last night! 

At 8:53pm, @__drewface called me and a few of his closest friends. He said that he'd arrived home to a flooded apartment. His wife was abroad, his baby daughter was freaking out, and he needed help ASAP before mold started growing

Within 10 minutes, we had 7 people on their way to his house. Soon after we had a coordinating WhatsApp group that grew to 14 people
@evodevotee was an hour away so she became the Guy In The Chair, using LLMs to come up with a checklist operating procedure for our converging team. She was joined by @madhu___s to figure out purchases of equipment from Home Depot

Meanwhile @MarkEstefanos took off on his electric skateboard to go pick them up

A big group of us show up all at once at the apartment. @IvanVendrov came with smoothies. @beana_tweets came with her boyfriend. I came with Poli, my rockstar friend visiting from Berlin
We went downstairs to assess the damage. The bottom floor was now a pond about 1inch deep. Lots of furniture, fabrics, and electronics were sitting in water 
The source of the flooding was a low-set window. The water had streamed in during the torrential downpour a couple hours previous

We got to work: 
• We created a human chain to move wet stuff to dry places. 
• In the absence of a mop, @beana_tweets used a broom to usher water into the floor drain we uncovered. 
• Poli mopped the floor; she used diluted bleach to clean away runoff water residue, making the floor fit for Andrew's baby to crawl on the next day

In parallel:
• @mr_samosaman went knocking on neighbor's doors to borrow a charge-card to operate the laundry machines
• @pee_zombie brought a wet/dry vacuum from @fractaltechnyc 
• I also put on music bc our crew's tacit philosophy is that work can be fun

Finally @MarkEstefanos arrived with the materials to finish the job. These included absorbent towels, gloves, moisture absorbing gel, and four fans that dried the mopped floors extremely fast

As the fans ran, I biked to a place nearby that has the best birria in Brooklyn and picked up tacos, tostadas, and mulitas

We ate them to celebrate 
(that's @MarkEstefanos holding the bag of birria)
In the end, @danielgolliher arrived to help, but we had no more tasks for him. Our crew of 10 had conquered the job in about 2hrs 

Some takeaways:
1. Supercoordinaion is possible: I came away impressed by:
• how many friends showed up
• the speed with which they arrived late on a Wednesday night
• how fluidly the group coordinated. No one stood around waiting to be directed – each person was independently sensing for what next things needed to be done. Then they did it, enlisting help if needed

2. LLMs are amazing in emergencies: We used them to quickly create plans, like: "Here's the situation: [context dump]. Come up with an operation procedure for a team of 8 amateurs to handle it." They also answered super specific questions on the fly, like "Should we turn off the HVAC system to prevent mold spores from traveling?"

3. The power of friendship: real

Additional thanks to Ian & Sunil, who wanted to volunteer but we already had too many people. Also to @feral_eyes, who lives all the way in CDMX but who volunteered to cover costs from afar

Btw in case you're reading this, thinking "Wow, there's some crazy magic or luck going on there" – you're wrong! 

My friends and I spent a few years figuring out the playbook for how to create a community where people actually show up for one another. I'll post the story of that below because I hope other folks find a way to replicate it. I want a society where ppl have each other's backs

title: How Prigoose got 22 friends to move nearby (and it worked)
summary:
Priya Rose (Prigoose) didn’t just post a “wouldn’t it be nice” fantasy—she dropped a reproducible playbook: how she got **22 friends within walking distance** in NYC, and why most groups never pull it off. The thread hit because it packaged something people already quietly crave (NathanpmYoung: “I would love to live walking distance from my closest friends”) into actual steps, plus a credible flex: this started *before* her Neighborhood NYC ambitions, and she’s basically treating 22-friends-nearby as the prototype for scaling to “what if it was 1000 people.” Drew (@__drewface) immediately turned it into FAQ-mode logistics—metrics like “**10–20 small social encounters per day**” and “**~50 friends each week**,” plus the unglamorous constraints (cheap place, roommates, patience, start with 1 unit then 2; “no, you don’t need to be wealthy”).

The arc is clean: **trigger → peak → outcome**. Trigger: Nathan’s 2022 “how do you do this?” tweet, with Drew previewing the tactics (roommates → acquire units → weekly dinners → publish the vision). Peak: Prigoose’s Feb 2023 viral “How to live near your friends” thread becomes the thing everyone points to—eshear calls it “practical steps,” Nathan quotes it as a jealousy object, and Drew adds the numbers to make it feel real. Outcome/current state: instead of backlash, it gets refined into a key warning label. When mbateman says most people just don’t prioritize walking-distance friendships (they’ll drive; suburbs win), Drew replies: don’t try to coordinate your *existing* friend group—**“plant a flag”** and build an overlapping group around shared preferences. That line basically becomes the anti-failure-mode patch.

And then it gets validated the way internet community theories almost never do: in Aug 2025, TylerAlterman posts the stress test—Drew comes home to a flooded apartment with a freaked-out baby, and within **10 minutes** seven friends are en route, a WhatsApp group spins up to 14, evodevotee plays remote ops lead using LLM-generated checklists, MarkEstefanos skateboards to Home Depot, IvanVendrov shows up with smoothies, and the whole thing is solved in ~2 hours with tacos at the end. People care because this thread turned “move near friends” from wistful posting into a meme + method (“you can just do things (with your friends!)”), and now it has the receipts: you’re not just optimizing vibes—you’re building a neighborhood that actually shows up when it matters.
